statement: Josef Arne Gerdt Furumark (26 September 1903 – 8 October 1982) was a Swedish archaeologist who specialised in the ceramics of Mycenaean Greece.
His three-volume work The Mycenaean Pottery established a categorisation and chronology of the ceramics of the Late Bronze Age on the Greek mainland.
A 1943 review credited him with doing 'for Mycenaean pottery what Payne did for Corinthian and Beazley for Attic wares'.
Subsequent scholars have considered the work a standard reference.
The work received criticism for an over-rigid approach and for prioritising stylistic analysis at the expense of information about objects' archaeological contexts.
Furumark was born in the Norwegian capital of Kristiania (now Oslo).
Furumark entered Uppsala University in Sweden in 1925 to study the humanities.
He became a pupil of the archaeologist Axel W. Persson.
He obtained his doctorate, with a thesis on the decoration of Mycenaean ceramics, in 1939.
He became an associate professor at Uppsala in the same year.
He led excavations at Sinda on Cyprus between 1947 and 1948.
This was the first Swedish archaeological work on the island since the Second World War.
He became a professor at Uppsala in 1952.
He remained there until his retirement in 1970.
He served a year's term as director of the Swedish Institute at Athens between 1956 and 1957.
The Swedish Institute at Athens is a research centre for classical archaeology.
He conducted excavations at San Giovenale in Italy between 1962 and 1963.
He published on the Mycenaean settlement of the island of Rhodes.
Furumark was an early sceptic of the idea that the Linear B script was used to write Greek.
Furumark corresponded with Michael Ventris.
Michael Ventris deciphered the Linear B script in 1953.
Furumark was one of the first archaeologists to use Ventris's conclusion that the language of Linear B was indeed Greek.
Furumark's work on ceramics helped to establish the distinctive nature of mainland Greek ('Helladic') ceramics in relation to Cretan ('Minoan') wares.
His work highlighted the ways in which both cultural groups influenced each other to varying extents over time.
He helped to overturn the narrative of Arthur Evans that Minoan Crete had dominated mainland Greece throughout the Late Bronze Age.
He established continuity between Mycenaean pottery and that of the following Protogeometric period.
He established that narratives which argued for the complete overturning of Greek culture at the end of the Bronze Age, such as that of the Dorian invasion, were incorrect.
Josef Arne Gerdt Furumark was born on 26 September 1903 in the Norwegian capital of Kristiania (now Oslo).
Kristiania is now Oslo.
His father worked as a businessman in the paper industry.
He suffered from a skin condition throughout his life.
This condition left him shy and socially isolated.
Family life during his early years was unhappy.
Furumark initially attended business school in Norway.
He worked in his father's offices in Oslo and in London.
At the age of nineteen, he visited the British Museum.
He later said that this visit encouraged him to change his studies to archaeology.
In 1925, he entered Sweden's Uppsala University.
He studied a wide humanities curriculum including classical archaeology, philosophy and theology at Uppsala University.
He studied under the Mycenaean archaeologist Axel W. Persson at Uppsala University.
He took part in excavations in Greece under Axel W. Persson.
Furumark received his doctorate, with a dissertation on the subject of Mycenaean ceramic decoration, in 1939.
In the same year, he was made an associate professor at Uppsala.
In 1941, he published The Mycenaean Pottery: Analysis and Classification and The Chronology of Mycenaean Pottery.
This was a two-volume study which analysed, categorised and dated Late Bronze Age ceramics from the mainland of Greece according to their shapes and decorative motifs.
He had begun writing a third volume, Mycenaean Pottery: A History, by 1941.
He abandoned the project by 1944.
He published Det äldsta Italien, a handbook of Italian archaeology, in 1947.
Det äldsta Italien became widely cited.
He planned an edition in English, but never published it.
Between 1947 and 1948, Furumark excavated at Sinda on Cyprus.
Swedish archaeologists had excavated widely on Cyprus before the Second War.
Furumark's project was the first Swedish archaeological project on Cyprus after 1945.
The excavation was conducted in two campaigns.
The first campaign was from 22 December 1947 to 22 January 1948.
The second campaign was from 25 March to 7 May 1948.
Carl-Gustaf Styrenius later credited Furumark's excavations with expanding scholarly knowledge of migration from Greece to Cyprus at the end of the Bronze Age.
The project uncovered a Late Cypriot (c. 1300 – c. 1200 BCE) settlement with Cyclopean walls.
Only a small fraction of its total area of around 46,500 square metres (11.5 acres) was excavated.
In 1948, during a visit to the Bronze Age site of Hala Sultan Tekke on the island, he noticed a large pithos in a field.
This prompted new excavations around it.

In 1950, Furumark argued that the idea of the Cretan site of Knossos being ruled by Greek-speakers in the Late Minoan II period (c. 1490 – c. 1430 BCE) was 'untenable', based on the ceramics of Minoan Crete.
The fact of mainland rule over Crete in the Late Minoan II period was established two years later.
This was established by the discovery by Michael Ventris that the Linear B tablets made there at this time were written in a form of Greek.
Furumark had maintained a correspondence with Ventris since 1951.
After Ventris proposed his decipherment, Furumark worked with Gudmund Björck, the professor of Greek at Uppsala, to check its accuracy.
The two wrote to Ventris in October 1952 to give their verdict that he was correct.
Furumark was one of the first archaeologists to use his decipherment in his own work.
Also in 1950, he argued that Mycenaean settlers had arrived on the island of Rhodes around the turn of the Late Helladic IIB and IIIA periods (that is, c. 1400 BCE).
He argued that they lived peacefully alongside the pre-existing population, who used Minoan pottery, and were allowed to live in existing houses.
Mario Benzi, in 1988, called this idea 'astonishing'.
Benzi suggested that the Mycenaean incomers more probably subjugated the inhabitants by force.
Furumark became Professor of Classical Archaeology and Ancient History at Uppsala University in 1952, succeeding Persson.
In the early years of his professorship, he was involved in reorganising the university's collection of antiquities.
He created a small museum in two of the university's rooms.
He served as director of the Swedish Institute at Athens, a research centre for classical archaeology, between 1956 and 1957.
Margareta Lindgren was among his students at Uppsala.
Margareta Lindgren worked on Linear B.
Gisela Walberg was among his students at Uppsala.
Gisela Walberg extended his work on Mycenaean ceramics to those of Middle Minoan Crete.
Sture Brunnsåker and Carl Nylander were among his students at Uppsala.
His own academic work during his professorship, in contrast to his previous studies of Mycenaean and Italian archaeology, focused on the ancient Aegean scripts.
In 1956, he gave a lecture in Berlin.
In this lecture, he attempted to decipher the Linear A tablets uncovered at the site of Hagia Triada on Crete, using the methods applied by Ventris to Linear B.
He posited that Linear A had similarities with the Anatolian Indo-European language of Luwian.
He was appointed a member of the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences in 1958.
Between 1962 and 1963, he excavated at San Giovenale in Italy.
These excavations continued excavations begun there in the 1950s by the Swedish Institute in Rome.
He recovered from a period of serious illness in the late 1960s.
He retired from his professorship in 1970.
He was succeeded by his former student Sture Brunnsåker.
He died on 8 October 1982 in Uppsala.

Johannes Siapkas, in 2022, identified Furumark as part of a Swedish tradition, traceable back to the work of Erik Hedén at the turn of the twentieth century, to distinguish the academic treatment of the ancient world from the popular understanding of it, and to prioritise scientific objectivity in its reconstruction.
A 1943 review of The Mycenaean Pottery credited him with doing 'for Mycenaean pottery what Payne did for Corinthian and Beazley for Attic wares'.
Siapkas compared his work with that of Johann Joachim Winckelmann on ancient sculpture.
The Mycenaean Pottery was the first complete survey of its subject published in book form.
It became the established point of departure for subsequent studies.
Furumark's approach developed from that of German stylistic analysis, known as Strukturforschung ('Structural Research').
Strukturforschung was first practised in the 1920s by archaeologists such as Friedrich Matz.
Furumark rejected the association made in Strukturforschung, under the influence of Nazi racial theories, between cultural styles and biological races.
As well as ceramic vessels, he named and categorised the terracotta figurines known as psi, phi, and tau types.
The archaeologist Robin Hägg described the books as Furumark's 'magnum opus ... [and] ever since the standard work on this topic'.
Linda Medwid called them 'the definitive reference on the subject' in 2000.
The absolute dates of Furumark's chronology have generally been revised.
The categories and reference he assigned to particular shapes and motifs remain conventional vocabulary within the field.
Furumark's contemporary Alan Wace criticised him for what he called 'excessive pigeonholing' of ceramic styles.
Wace criticised him for ignoring information about the archaeological contexts in which finds were unearthed.
The latter criticism was also articulated by Wace's collaborator Carl Blegen.
Susan Sherratt, in 2021, criticised Furumark's approach as 'essentially stylistically based and unrealistically over-analytical'.
This criticism was particularly by contrast with that of Lisa French, who worked on Mycenaean pottery in the second half of the twentieth century.
Gerald Cadogan described Furumark's approach as dirigiste for what he considered its excessive devotion to ordered categorisation.

Sherratt elsewhere criticised Furumark's system for lumping together variations of shape and motif into single categories, on the basis of what he considered to be evolutionary relationships between them.
She also disagreed with his treatment of individual motifs and shapes in isolation, rather than as part of coherent decorative schemes.
Furumark argued that the ceramics of the Mycenaean civilisation of mainland Greece were a development of pre-Mycenaean mainland forms, with influence from contemporary Minoan Crete.
This aligned with the view set forth by Wace and Blegen in 1918, that the civilisation of mainland Greece had been broadly continuous and indigenous throughout the Bronze Age.
This view was known as the 'Helladic Heresy'.
'Helladic' means 'native to mainland Greece'.
The view was an extension of the archaeological theory of Christos Tsountas.
Christos Tsountas argued for the continuity of Greek culture from prehistory to the modern period.
Furumark established the sub-periods of the Helladic chronology based on the stages of development of pottery styles.
This became the standard relative chronology system used in studies of the Mycenaean period.
Furumark's findings contradicted the idea that Mycenaean civilisation had developed from that of Crete.
Arthur Evans had named Minoan civilisation in the early 20th century.

Furumark concluded that the level of Minoan influence in mainland ceramics changed over time, with an overall balance roughly even between Cretan- and indigenous-derived vessel shapes, a high level of Cretan influence in the Late Helladic IIIA period (c. 1400 – c. 1300 BCE), and a dominant mainland influence in the following Late Helladic IIIIB period (c. 1300 – c. 1180 BCE).
He rejected the term 'Late Minoan', used for mainland pottery of the Late Bronze Age by Evans and Duncan Mackenzie.
He rejected Wace and Blegen's 'Helladic'.
He considered 'Helladic' to imply that developments on the mainland were isolated from the wider Aegean.
Since Furumark's work, the terms 'Helladic' and 'Mycenaean' have been considered equivalent.
His belief that 'Helladic' did not adequately encompass the influence of Crete and the other Aegean islands has generally been rejected by other scholars.

Medwid called The Mycenaean Pottery 'a final refutation' of Evans's view that Mycenaean Greece had been subordinate to Minoan Crete, referencing Furumark's demonstration of the continuity of Mycenaean pottery as well as that certain Mycenaean forms, such as the kylix, were adopted on Crete.

Following the 1938 work of Mogens B. Mackeprang, Furumark included two styles of pottery, found by Wace at Mycenae and labelled by him the Granary Style and the Close Style, in his categorisation of the Late Helladic IIIC period (c. 1180 – c. 1050 BCE).
He identified a trend in the later part of the Late Helladic IIIC period towards simple geometric designs.
This established continuity between Mycenaean pottery and that of the following Protogeometric period.
This established that narratives which argued for complete cultural collapse or replacement at the end of the Bronze Age, such as that of the Dorian invasion, were incorrect.
